items.title: To End Global Hunger, Invest in Rural Communities
items.author: Esther Ngumbi
items.description: Even as hunger declines around the world, food insecurity remains prevalent in rural communities. Restoring soil health, expanding access to new technologies, strengthening land rights, and upgrading public infrastructure are essential to boost agricultural productivity and protect rural livelihoods.

items.title: The Sanctions Illusion
items.author: Jamal Ibrahim Haidar
items.description: Those who defend sweeping financial sanctions against countries like Russia and Iran often claim that popular suffering is a defensible means of pressuring the target government. But while such measures certainly inflict widespread suffering on civilian populations, this rarely translates into political change.

items.title: Is Monetarism Making a Comeback?
items.author: Tim Congdon
items.description: After decades on the margins of mainstream economic thinking, monetarism is beginning to re-enter the debate, most notably at the Federal Reserve. To regain credibility, however, monetarists must learn from past mistakes and adapt to the monetary and financial realities of the 21st century.

items.title: China’s Super-Dam Is Becoming an Upstream Water Bomb
items.author: Brahma Chellaney
items.description: The latest evidence suggests that the Chinese scientific establishment understands the dangers of a planned Himalayan dam—the world's largest—more clearly than its political leadership is willing to acknowledge. With the livelihoods of two billion people at stake, the international community needs to weigh in.

items.title: Europe and the War in Ukraine
items.author: Joschka Fischer
items.description: If Europe remains a mere collection of small states and middle powers, the current period of profound geopolitical and historical change will also mark the end of its role on the world stage. With no end in sight for Russia's war in Ukraine, Europeans must come to grips with reality.

items.title: Europe Must Stand with Canada Against Trump
items.author: Philippe Legrain
items.description: Rather than keeping their heads down as US President Donald Trump wages another trade war with Canada, European leaders must recognize that they could be next. Like Canada, the European Union is a middle power whose future prosperity and security will depend on solidarity with economic peers.

items.title: Is China Really a Champion of the Global South?
items.author: Adekeye Adebajo
items.description: The United States is an overextended hegemon, and its decline will continue slowly, as other powers like China assume more global responsibilities. Against this backdrop, China’s efforts to lead the Global South are more about consolidating its power in the current international system than creating a new one that benefits all.

items.title: The Economist’s Embarrassing Proxy War Over AI Policy
items.author: Eran Yashiv
items.description: The disagreements between the Nobel laureate economist Daron Acemoglu and his opponents are consequential—and so are the opponents. But rather than engage in good faith with Acemoglu's arguments, the venerable British news magazine recently stooped to bibulous calumny by unnamed critics of his work.

items.title: Democracies Must Get Serious About Industrial Policy
items.author: Ngaire Woods
items.description: For decades, Western governments have ceded the strategic direction of their economies to the market. To dominate the industries of the future, they must learn from their own history and rebuild the institutions, expertise, and discipline that effective industrial policy demands.

items.title: In the AI Gold Rush, the Cloud Wins
items.author: Cecilia Rikap
items.description: Even if the AI investment boom turns out to have been a bubble, the Big Tech companies that have cornered the cloud infrastructure market will emerge as strong as ever, or even stronger. That is why Amazon, Microsoft, and Google are in a league of their own, even compared to other giants like Meta and Nvidia.

items.title: Don’t Mess With Markets
items.author: Stephen S. Roach
items.description: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has justified his intervention in currency and bond markets by arguing that they are not providing a fair signal of economic fundamentals. But they are, and Bessent's willingness to peddle such nonsense may be the most striking testament yet to the sycophancy that defines the Trump administration.

items.title: Kevin Warsh Owes Us an Apology
items.author: Marco Buti
items.description: After only a few months in office, the chair of the US Federal Reserve has left market participants disoriented and confused. His first address to the annual monetary-policy symposium in Jackson Hole is an opportunity to set things aright—or to make matters even worse.

items.title: Is the Trump Treasury Panicking?
items.author: Kenneth Rogoff
items.description: With the federal deficit near 6% of GDP and the national debt surpassing $40 trillion, America’s fiscal position looks increasingly precarious. By trying to strong-arm the bond market rather than address the underlying problem, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent may have squandered his hard-earned credibility.

items.title: What the World’s Oldest Bank Reveals About EU Financial Integration
items.author: Lucrezia Reichlin
items.description: To fend off an attempted takeover, Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena has launched its own bids for two other Italian banks. The episode shows why EU policymakers should focus less on making governments surrender their influence over national banking systems and more on building a European financing channel.

items.title: The Age of Gated Recessions
items.author: Kaushik Basu
items.description: Aggregate economic indicators are obscuring a widening divide between those enjoying rapid income growth and those facing deteriorating job prospects. The rise of AI could deepen this disparity, with certain regions and workers experiencing recession-like conditions while others enjoy boom times.

items.title: The AI Curse
items.author: Stephen Holmes
items.description: Every sanction that ordinary citizens have ever possessed—the ability to withhold labor, taxes, sons, or votes—presupposes someone who needs what you can withhold. As AI infrastructure encroaches on Americans, they are learning the lesson of many resource-rich states: where there is no need, there is no democracy.

items.title: Where Will the Global Bond Rout Hit Growth and Equities?
items.author: Nouriel Roubini
items.description: In the US, the recent rise in bond yields is largely driven by structural factors like the end of the post-2008 Great Stagnation, higher potential growth from tech-industry investments, and greater private-sector demand for credit. Higher yields are more worrisome for advanced economies that are stagnating and innovating less.

items.title: Trump’s Korean Catastrophe
items.author: Richard Haass
items.description: Donald Trump seems not to appreciate that deterrence depends on the ability to mount a credible defense. This makes the Korean Peninsula a more dangerous place, not least because 28,000 US troops are stationed in South Korea, which the US is obliged by treaty to defend.

items.title: The Dollar’s Outer Defenses Have Been Breached
items.author: Harold James
items.description: The puzzle of why the Trump administration is so concerned with a falling yen has historical parallels not to the 1930s or the 1980s, but to the 1960s, when US officials feared that a crisis elsewhere could spread to America. With US bond yields spiking, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is getting desperate.

items.title: Why the World Still Needs Wall Street
items.author: Jorge Arbache
items.description: Outside of the United States, all other financial systems face major constraints on their ability to absorb large financial inflows. That is why geopolitical multipolarity is advancing faster than financial multipolarity, despite the many reasons that investors have to pursue greater diversification.

items.title: Aging Populations Need Not Mean Frailer Economies
items.author: Andrew J. Scott
items.description: Governments and economists have long viewed demographic aging as a threat to economic growth. But new research finds that labor scarcity encourages investment and shifts innovation toward labor-saving technologies, boosting productivity enough to offset a shrinking workforce.

items.title: Who’s Afraid of Chinese Surpluses?
items.author: PS Commentators
items.description: China recorded the largest trade surplus in history last year, and its exports continue to grow. But the scale of the threat to the global economy, and the appropriate response, remains subject to considerable disagreement. Some economists advocate protectionist measures, if only to pressure China to commit to economic rebalancing, others argue that tariffs won’t help, and still others think the specter of another “China shock” is a bogeyman, because China’s surpluses do more good than harm.

items.title: The Big Picture
items.author: PS editors

items.title: Only Protectionism Can Safeguard European Industry
items.author: Desmond Lachman
items.description: While economic rebalancing by China would be good for everyone, Chinese leaders have given little indication that they are moving decisively in this direction. With China's ever-increasing exports threatening to decimate European manufacturing, the EU has little choice but to embrace tariffs.

items.title: The Gospel of the Great Leader
items.author: Yoon Young-kwan
items.description: North Korea’s communist regime has long functioned as a faith, repurposing Christian doctrine and imagery to deify its founder, Kim Il-sung, and his descendants. A new book traces how those religious influences transformed the Kim dynasty’s personality cult into a system that has endured across three generations.

items.title: Technology Is Not Above the Law
items.author: Olivier Sylvain
items.description: In arguing for a regulatory regime that is skewed entirely toward freeing developers to build online services, rather than placing any social obligations on them, the AI industry is using a playbook that Silicon Valley wrote 30 years ago. This time, however, the public seems less inclined to buy the industry's argument.

items.title: Superintelligent Democracy
items.author: Audrey Tang
items.description: Rather than framing the pursuit of AI capabilities as a race, we should turn the process into a democratic mission, with milestones set by the people, rather than on their behalf. Taiwan's own demonstration of mission-led governance, along with insights from the open-web community, show what is possible.

items.title: China’s Platform State and the AI Race
items.author: Angela Huyue Zhang
items.description: Balancing regulation with innovation is never easy, and the Chinese government’s robust support for AI could lead to inefficiency and excess. But the “platform state” model, combined with other strengths, has enabled China to achieve dominance in multiple strategic sectors, while enhancing its resilience.

items.title: Which Future for Online Life?
items.author: Carissa Véliz
items.description: By articulating a vision of the future that seems inevitable, technology industry leaders want to create the impression that the surrender of privacy and other defining trends of the current moment cannot be stopped. But predictions become self-fulfilling prophecies only if we believe them and act accordingly.

items.title: Europe’s Pro-Human Vision
items.author: Margrethe Vestager
items.description: The original vision of the internet as a democratizing force failed to account for the manner in which power would concentrate, attention would be monetized, and public discourse would be manipulated. In Europe and elsewhere, these lessons now must inform how we govern generative AI.

items.title: Will We Preserve the Sources of Human Learning?
items.author: Zena Hitz
items.description: By obscuring or destroying the primary sources of knowledge, large language models create the illusion of an embodied and active collection of everything we know. But without examining and interrogating the human originators of recorded knowledge and wisdom, one cannot fully develop one’s own understanding.

items.title: How Europe Can Save a Trillion Euros and Win the AI Race
items.author: Eric Hazan
items.description: If the risk Europe faces is losing access to frontier AI models, the solution is not necessarily to chase the labs that created them in the hopes of eventually pulling ahead. Instead, it is to build the capacity to make surviving that loss possible, such as by investing in AI infrastructure and training capabilities.

items.title: MDBs Are Becoming a New Global Safe Asset
items.author: Erik Berglöf
items.description: Even as multilateralism faces an existential threat, multilateral development banks are not only surviving but thriving. Thanks to MDBs’ ability to borrow at costs close to that of the US Treasury, they have created a new class of de facto risk-free assets that could help underpin the global financial system.

items.title: Why US Bond Markets Are Trembling
items.author: Jim O'Neill
items.description: What is the apparent fragility in the US bond market telling us? Since markets tend to be less wrong than those who comment on them regularly, their signals must be taken seriously, especially when they coincide with a relative softening in US inflation figures and other high-frequency economic indicators.

items.title: Look East for Lessons in Democratic Resistance
items.author: Jeffrey N. Wasserstrom
items.description: Pro-democracy activists often turn to Eastern and Central Europe for inspiration, while Asia’s remarkable democratic breakthroughs receive far less attention. Yet the continent’s recent struggles offer valuable lessons for those seeking to resist the global advance of authoritarianism.

items.title: Three Ways AI Will Change the Course of Humanity
items.author: Dambisa Moyo
items.description: The AI debate has largely focused on productivity gains and job displacement, but its consequences will reach much further By revolutionizing how we combat disease, wage wars, and stimulate income growth, AI could fundamentally alter the terms of human existence.

items.title: Global Economic Convergence Is Stalling
items.author: Keun Lee
items.description: For a while, the world’s advanced economies (other than the US) were rapidly losing ground to their emerging counterparts. But the BRICS' catch-up momentum has stalled since 2016, not because the G7 has been doing better, but because everyone has been doing worse.

items.title: When a Big Energy Project Turns Bad
items.author: Djoomart Otorbaev
items.description: After hundreds of millions of dollars were invested by developing-country governments, and before a single watt of energy was transferred, the CASA-1000 infrastructure project in Central Asia has effectively failed. The international institutions that conceived, financed, and promoted the project must answer for this.

items.title: The Trolling of American Democracy
items.author: Robert Gulotty
items.description: Democracy is most vulnerable when voters can no longer distinguish genuine abuses of power from partisan attacks. Authoritarian leaders exploit that uncertainty by blurring the line between misconduct and political theater, making legitimate criticism look like just another witch hunt.

items.title: A Future With Chinese Characteristics
items.author: Mark Leonard
items.description: The world is undergoing a historical and cultural rupture. Just as Hollywood and other American exports once gave the rest of the world a glimpse of modern life and the future that awaited them, China is now doing the same for African, Latin American, and even American young people.

items.title: Putin Has Run Out of Moves
items.author: Anders Åslund
items.description: Even with the Russian economy suffering from low growth, high inflation, and relentless Ukrainian long-range drone strikes on energy infrastructure, President Vladimir Putin has thrown fiscal caution to the wind and allowed the government’s budget deficit to balloon to 2.8% of GDP. It isn’t likely to end well.

items.title: The Geopolitical Drag on AI Governance
items.author: Gabriela Ramos
items.description: The Trump administration’s decision to prioritize national competitiveness over multilateral frameworks has deepened the fragmentation of AI governance—and expanded the opening for China to organize its own system. But China's approach is similarly shaped primarily by its own geopolitical ambitions.

items.title: The Myth of the China Shock
items.author: Michael R. Strain
items.description: As advances in generative AI continue, US policymakers should heed two lessons from the opening of trade with China. But that will require them to rethink the conventional wisdom about deindustrialization and the decline of manufacturing employment.

items.title: Guatemala’s Democratic Renewal
items.author: Carlos Alvarado-Quesada
items.description: Guatemalan President Bernardo Arévalo’s recent selection of an honest successor to a corrupt attorney general represents a decisive victory for the country’s democracy. Arévalo succeeded not because he abandoned institutions to save democracy, but because he trusted institutions enough to work through them.

items.title: Iceland Belongs in the Eurozone
items.author: Willem H. Buiter
items.description: In evaluating the trade-offs of joining the European Union and giving up their own currency, Icelanders must recognize that the costs of eurozone membership are smaller than what past data suggest. If anything, being within the eurosystem would make a repeat of Iceland's post-2008 banking crisis exceedingly unlikely.

items.title: Zhu Rongji’s Legacy of Demographic Decline
items.author: Yi Fuxian
items.description: Former Chinese Premier Zhu Rongji’s recent death elicited widespread accolades for his role in pushing the market-oriented reforms that unleashed decades of economic growth. But Zhu also oversaw two major policy shifts that have had dire implications for China’s demographic outlook.

items.title: The Global Land Agenda’s Moment of Truth
items.author: Osama Faqeeha
items.description: As delegates gather this week in Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia, for the 17th Conference of the Parties (COP17) to the UN Convention to Combat Desertification, momentum is building toward a more ambitious global response to land degradation. In fact, there are five promising signs that this time could be different.

items.title: How Trump Is Reinvigorating Democracy
items.author: Jan-Werner Mueller
items.description: After a year of commentators lamenting the extent to which Donald Trump had emboldened the world’s autocrats, the political tables may have begun to turn. Not only is Trump deeply unpopular globally, but any government that gets into bed with him is effectively offering proof of its own corruption.

items.title: Ebola is Back-and the IMF’s Relief Fund Is Empty
items.author: Marina Zucker-Marques
items.description: Once again, the International Monetary Fund finds itself begging for resources to support poor countries facing a public-health emergency. It is an old problem, but one for which there is a remarkably simple solution.

items.title: What Should Be Done About Asia’s Undervalued Currencies?
items.author: Jeffrey Frankel
items.description: Those who worry that the renminbi, yen, and won are undervalued vis-à-vis the dollar are usually focused on the large trade and current-account surpluses that China, Japan, and Korea run with the US. But coordinated intervention in currency markets will not address the fundamentals underlying these imbalances.

items.title: How Corporations Can Mitigate an AI Jobocalypse
items.author: Raghuram G. Rajan
items.description: Even if AI-related job displacement is less severe than many feared, corporations will need to be enlisted in minimizing its effects in the name of social solidarity. To that end, governments should consider what policy incentives are in place, and large employers should consider their own long-term interests.

items.title: The Making and Remaking of Chinese Totalitarianism
items.author: Chenggang Xu
items.description: For decades, the West assumed that economic growth would turn China into a more open, liberal society, much as it did South Korea and Taiwan. Instead, China’s totalitarian institutions proved remarkably resilient, surviving decades of reform and reasserting themselves under President Xi Jinping.

items.title: Let’s Not Forget Multilateral Institutions
items.author: Anne-Marie Slaughter
items.description: The roadmap for middle-power action that Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Finnish President Alexander Stubb recently laid out calls for countries that share interests to create ad hoc coalitions. But to be effective, these coalitions must work as much as possible within existing multilateral institutions.

items.title: The Real Competitiveness Test
items.author: Jan Mischke
items.description: The balance of global investment has shifted dramatically over the past three decades, with China emerging as the leading destination for productive capital. Europe and the United States can still narrow the gap, but only by making it cheaper and easier to build, operate, and innovate.

items.title: Our AI, Your Problem
items.author: Bertrand Badré
items.description: The debate over whether European firms should use a Chinese state-directed model or one built by a private US firm threatens to distract from Europe’s most pressing problem, which is that it has no seat at either table. To preserve its own sovereignty, the continent must create a third option for itself.

items.title: Chile’s Boring Conservative President
items.author: Andrés Velasco
items.description: Rather than governing like a pugnacious populist or a ruthless pragmatist, Chile’s new president, José Antonio Kast, has adopted an old-school center-right agenda and governing style reminiscent of the 1980s. Yet even this potentially safer approach comes with its own risks and costs.

items.title: Europe Failed the Ceuta Test
items.author: Zaki Laïdi
items.description: The current migration crisis is eating away at the solidarity on which the European Union depends, fueling the rise of the far right and pushing leaders to adopt increasingly hardline policies. But the Ceuta debacle shows why such measures cannot address the deeper forces driving migration.

items.title: The Legacy of Zhu Rongji
items.author: Minxin Pei
items.description: Zhu Rongji’s personal history and political challenges made it highly unlikely that he would rise to the pinnacle of Chinese politics. Once there, he implemented many of the reforms that turned the country into an economic powerhouse.

items.title: The Twilight of the ICC
items.author: Shlomo Ben-Ami
items.description: Born amid the euphoria of the West’s Cold War victory, the International Criminal Court embodied the aspiration that international law could transcend politics. But the ICC always represented victors’ justice, and it was never equipped to operate in a world shaped by Machtpolitik.

items.title: Will Latin America Embrace Guerrilla Geopolitics?
items.author: Jorge G. Castañeda
items.description: The resurgence of guerrilla warfare in Ukraine and Iran has underscored the potential benefits of asymmetric action in today’s increasingly multipolar world. Latin America, in particular, should consider how to leverage its many strengths to remedy its relatively weak position on the global stage.

items.title: China’s Biggest Weakness on AI
items.author: Carl Benedikt Frey
items.description: When a state can credibly promise that labor displacement will not mean destitution, workers and their representatives are more likely to accept technological change. But since China can promise no such thing, its lack of a robust welfare state has emerged as a fundamental weakness in the broader AI race.

items.title: The Monetary Roots of Political Extremism
items.author: Ann Pettifor
items.description: While the global economy generates unprecedented wealth for plutocrats like Elon Musk, it is, by design, highly unequal, dangerously over-indebted, prone to recurring financial crises, and ecologically disastrous. In such a context, radical reforms will be needed, beginning with the rejection of money as a commodity.

items.title: The Return of the Power Trust
items.author: Sandeep Vaheesan
items.description: A century ago, the US power industry was dominated by sprawling, heavily indebted holding companies until their collapse forced the federal government to break them up. Now, the pattern is repeating, with mega-mergers and buyouts advancing a debt-heavy business model at the expense of households and communities.

items.title: Morocco’s Bet on Targeted AI
items.author: Amal El Fallah Seghrouchni
items.description: Rather than join the global race for computing power, Morocco has focused on building sovereignty over its data, talent, and uses of AI, because technological power will be measured by usefulness, not by domination. This strategy calls for the country to embrace innovation without ceding its identity to foreign models.

items.title: Dude, Where’s My Recession?
items.author: Barry Eichengreen
items.description: Despite a series of major negative shocks, some of them unprecedented, the US economy continues to grow in line with its estimated long-run potential. Yet given obvious and mounting risks, from debt-financed speculation to geopolitical tensions, the appearance of resilience should not be confused with the real thing.

items.title: The Rise of the Token Economy
items.author: Yaniv Benhamou
items.description: Millions of people continuously generate the raw material on which AI is trained, yet almost none shares in the wealth it creates. This underscores the need for data cooperatives representing internet users, creators, and other rights holders to negotiate access to the content being fed to large language models.

items.title: Excess Savings Are Driving the New China Shock
items.author: Daniel Gros
items.description: The current China shock combines continued supply upgrading with an absorption problem: the decline in property and related investment has reduced domestic demand, but national saving remains very high. The result is a larger savings-investment surplus that spills into net exports.

items.title: The World Economy Is Swerving, and the Destination Is Unknown
items.author: Mohamed A. El-Erian
items.description: The days of unfettered globalization, multilateral rule of law, commonly accepted limits on economic statecraft, and widely shared macroeconomic objectives are now long gone. A perpetual, directionless transition is our new reality, and corporate executives, investors, and policymakers must adapt accordingly.

items.title: Is China Really a Beggar-thy-Neighbor Power?
items.author: Dani Rodrik
items.description: When major economies are running at near full capacity, it is not clear that trade deficits should be a cause for concern, since they represent a transfer of purchasing power from surplus countries. Under the current circumstances, then, China’s widely criticized surpluses might as well be called enrich-thy-neighbor.
